system:
You audit the knowledge atoms of one Knowledge Card. A card is the answer key for a benchmark of expert conceptual knowledge, so every atom must be correct, self-contained, and assessable on its own.

Judge every atom on every check listed below. Rules:
- For checks about evidence, use only the evidence sentences supplied with the atom. Do not repair an atom with your own knowledge.
- Evidence text comes from a PDF text layer. If symbols are garbled so that you cannot verify the atom, answer "hold" for that check and say so.
- Be strict. When unsure between pass and a non-pass value, choose the non-pass value and explain.
- "why" is required for every value other than the first listed value; keep it under 30 words. Omit "why" when passing.

Checks (allowed values in brackets; the first value means no problem):
- GROUNDED [pass / revise / fail]: The cited evidence sentences state the atom. pass = fully stated. revise = the core claim is stated, and the gap is only wording, strength, or a dropped/extra peripheral qualifier that can be fixed by deleting or softening words (say what). fail = not stated, OR the atom adds substantive content the evidence lacks: a scope or population restriction (e.g. 'In B-ALL'), a mechanism or operation, a characterization (e.g. 'an unbounded while loop'), or a formula/definition. If deleting the unsupported part would change what the atom tests, it is fail, not revise. For pass, put the supporting evidence ids in cite (required).
- SINGLE_CLAIM [pass / revise]: The atom is one independently assessable claim. revise = it joins two or more claims that could be true or false separately.
- SCOPE_LABEL [pass / revise]: The S label fits (S1 what it is / S2 how it works / S3 where it ends). revise = wrong label; put the right one in why, e.g. 'S2: ...'.
- L1_ONLY [pass / revise / fail]: The atom is recall-level knowledge: one fact a person who studied the concept would simply know. revise = the core fact is recall-level but the sentence carries extra load that must be removed, e.g. stacked conditions (since/although/if ... and ...), a procedural or evaluative add-on ('easy to define but requires checking ...'), or a clause that introduces a second technical concept that must be known separately (e.g. 'if X is an inner Kan complex' when that is not the card concept). fail = knowing it requires applying the concept to a new problem, or combining facts from distant passages.
- SOURCE_INDEPENDENT [pass / revise / fail]: A domain expert who never read this book could judge the claim true or false. revise = phrased as the authors' statement but the claim itself is general (drop the attribution). fail = the authors' opinion or choice, or the finding of one study, so the answer is not fixed without the source.
- NO_OVERLAP [pass / fail]: No other atom in this card states or contains the same claim. If two atoms overlap, fail only the less informative one and put the other atom's id in cite; the other one passes.
- CENTRALITY [pass / fail]: The atom matters for understanding the concept. fail = peripheral detail.
Whole-card checks (report under "batch"):
- CONCEPT_SCOPE [pass / fail]: The concept is a general concept of the field. fail = a single system, product, or one study's topic.

Output ONLY one JSON object:
{"units": {"<atom_id>": {"<CHECK>": {"v": "<value>", "why": "", "cite": []}, ...}, ...}, "batch": {"<CHECK>": {"v": "<value>", "why": ""}}}
user:
CONCEPT: atomic_ref
ASSESSMENT SCOPE: Covers the atomic_ref class: non-owning semantics derived from C++20 std::atomic_ref, DefaultOrder/DefaultScope/address-space template arguments, use with buffers and USM, and the rule against mixing atomic and non-atomic access. Excludes the deprecated SYCL 1.2.1 atomic class except as contrast.

ATOMS:
- DPCPP2-C03-S1-01 | S1
  ATOM: Creating an atomic reference acts as a promise that the referenced variable will only be accessed atomically for the lifetime of that reference.
  EVIDENCE:
    [DPCPP2-p0564-s04] Creating an atomic reference effectively acts as a promise that the referenced variable will only be accessed atomically for the lifetime of the reference.
- DPCPP2-C03-S1-02 | S1
  ATOM: In SYCL kernels, the atomic_ref class is based on C++20 std::atomic_ref, whose instances do not own their data but are constructed from an existing non-atomic variable.
  EVIDENCE:
    [DPCPP2-p0564-s03] The biggest difference between the two classes is that instances of std::atomic_ref do not own their data but are instead constructed from an existing non-atomic variable.
    [DPCPP2-p0564-s06] The atomic_ref class used in SYCL kernels is therefore based on std::atomic_ref.
- DPCPP2-C03-S1-03 | S1
  ATOM: The SYCL atomic_ref class replaces the cl::sycl::atomic class from SYCL 1.2.1, which is deprecated in SYCL 2020, and the atomic_ref class should be used in its place.
  EVIDENCE:
    [DPCPP2-p0563-s14] The cl::sycl::atomic class is deprecated in SYCL 2020.
    [DPCPP2-p0563-s15] The
    [DPCPP2-p0563-s16] atomic_ref class (covered in the next section) should be used in its place.
- DPCPP2-C03-S2-01 | S2
  ATOM: SYCL atomic_ref lets the programmer set the default memory order and memory scope as part of the object's type through the DefaultOrder and DefaultScope template arguments, as a compromise between C++ defaults and lowest-common-denominator defaults.
  EVIDENCE:
    [DPCPP2-p0565-s03] The design adopted by SYCL offers a compromise, allowing us to define our desired default behavior as part of an object’s type (using the DefaultOrder and DefaultScope template arguments).
    [DPCPP2-p0565-s04] Other orderings and scopes can be provided as runtime arguments to specific atomic operations as we see fit—the DefaultOrder and DefaultScope only impact operations where we do not or cannot override the default behavior (e.g., when using a shorthand operator like +=).
- DPCPP2-C03-S2-02 | S2
  ATOM: DefaultOrder and DefaultScope affect only atomic_ref operations whose behavior is not or cannot be overridden, such as shorthand operators like +=, because other orderings and scopes can be passed as runtime arguments to specific operations.
  EVIDENCE:
    [DPCPP2-p0565-s04] Other orderings and scopes can be provided as runtime arguments to specific atomic operations as we see fit—the DefaultOrder and DefaultScope only impact operations where we do not or cannot override the default behavior (e.g., when using a shorthand operator like +=).
- DPCPP2-C03-S2-03 | S2
  ATOM: Because atomic_ref wraps an existing non-atomic variable, non-atomic data can be created on the host, transferred to the device, and treated as atomic data only after the transfer.
  EVIDENCE:
    [DPCPP2-p0564-s05] These are exactly the semantics needed by SYCL, since they allow us to create non-atomic data on the host, transfer that data to the device, and treat it as atomic data only after it has been transferred.
- DPCPP2-C03-S2-04 | S2
  ATOM: To use atomic operations with buffers in SYCL, a buffer of non-atomic data is created and transferred to the device, and that data is then accessed through an atomic reference.
  EVIDENCE:
    [DPCPP2-p0568-s04] To use atomic operations in conjunction with buffers, we must create a buffer of non-atomic data to be transferred to the device and then access that data through an atomic reference.
- DPCPP2-C03-S3-01 | S3
  ATOM: While any atomic_ref referencing a specific object exists, all accesses to that object must occur atomically via an instance of atomic_ref.
  EVIDENCE:
    [DPCPP2-p0569-s06] When mixing atomic and non-atomic accesses like this, it is important to pay attention to object lifetimes—while any atomic_ref referencing a specific object exists, all accesses to that object must occur (atomically) via an instance of atomic_ref.
- DPCPP2-C03-S3-02 | S3
  ATOM: Unlike atomic_ref, std::atomic cannot be used in SYCL device kernels because its instances own their data and cannot be moved or copied, so atomic objects cannot be created on the host and transferred to the device; attempting to use it in a kernel causes a compiler error.
  EVIDENCE:
    [DPCPP2-p0563-s07] Instances of the atomic class own their data, cannot be moved or copied, and can only be updated using atomic operations.
    [DPCPP2-p0563-s09] Unfortunately, they also prevent the class from being used in SYCL kernels—it is impossible to create atomic objects on the host and transfer them to the device!
    [DPCPP2-p0563-s10] We are free to continue using std::atomic in our host code, but attempting to use it inside of device kernels will result in a compiler error.
- DPCPP2-C03-S3-03 | S3
  ATOM: Atomicity guarantees do not apply if only some of the concurrent accesses to a memory location use atomics, and mixing atomic and non-atomic operations on the same location at the same time results in undefined behavior.
  EVIDENCE:
    [DPCPP2-p0551-s04] Note that this guarantee does not apply if only some of the accesses use atomics and that it is our responsibility as programmers to ensure that we do not concurrently access the same data using operations with different atomicity guarantees.
    [DPCPP2-p0551-s05] Mixing atomic and non-atomic operations on the same memory location(s) at the same time results in undefined behavior!
